doc.title: Oven temperature calibration

pages.title: Oven temperature calibration

content.text: The crust color kept coming out paler than the books describe, so I measured what the oven actually does.
Oven thermometer on the middle rack, center
Dial set to 200, 230 and 250 °C; after 20 minutes of preheating, read the thermometer
Every setting runs 14–16 °C below the dial. The offset is nearly constant
Opening the door drops it by almost 30 °C, and it takes 5 minutes to recover
When a recipe says 230 °C, set the dial to 245 °C
Preheat at least 20 minutes before loading. Keep the door open as briefly as possible
The "230 °C" in trials 1–7 was really about 215 °C. That explains the pale crust

doc.title: Reading notes - hydration and crumb structure

pages.title: Reading notes - hydration and crumb structure

content.text: Notes from a baking textbook and a flour mill's technical sheet on how hydration relates to crumb structure.
Hydration is the weight of water as a share of the flour weight. Typical ranges: 60–70% for sandwich loaves, 70–80% for hearth breads
More water makes the dough softer and more extensible, so the gas from fermentation grows into larger cells. That is why the crumb "opens"
Whether the dough can hold the water depends on the amount and quality of protein (gluten). Higher-protein flour absorbs more water, so at the same hydration the dough is tighter
Rule of thumb: a 1% difference in protein shifts absorption by about 2%. 75% on an 11% flour is roughly like 78–79% on a 12.5% flour
High-hydration dough builds gluten better through rests and folds than through kneading. An autolyse (flour and water rested first) also helps
Push hydration too far and the gluten network cannot support the water: the dough slackens, the loaf bakes flat, and the crumb ends up tighter, not more open
Raising hydration from 65 to 75% in trials 1–3 opened the crumb because the bread flour had enough protein
The failure with the lower-protein flour ("spreads sideways, dense bottom") is exactly the slackening described here

doc.title: Reading notes - fermentation temperature and time

pages.title: Reading notes - fermentation temperature and time

content.text: Notes on sourdough fermentation temperature and time, from a book and from the baker who shared the starter with me.
Bulk fermentation is best at 24–27 °C. With 20% starter, expect the dough to double in 4–5 hours in that range
Each 1 °C rise speeds fermentation by roughly 10–15%. At 28 °C it runs about 30% faster than at 26 °C
Above 28 °C the acid-producing bacteria take over and the dough turns sour. Acid also weakens gluten, so an overblown dough collapses easily
Cold fermentation at 4–6 °C for 8–16 hours nearly stops the rise, but enzymes keep working and build aroma and sweetness. Cold dough is also easier to shape
Judge the end of fermentation by volume and the spring-back of a poke, not by the clock. Recipe times mean nothing once the temperature changes
Trial 4 (28 °C, 4 hours) collapsed because I let the clock, not the dough, decide. At 28 °C I should have stopped at 3 hours
The better flavor of trial 5 (12 hours cold) matches the cold-fermentation effect described here

content.text: Hydration is defined as the weight of water expressed as a percentage of the flour weight
Typical hydration ranges are 60–70 % for sandwich loaves and 70–80 % for hearth breads
Adding water makes the dough softer and more extensible, allowing fermentation gas to expand into larger cells and thereby opening the crumb

The amount of water a dough can retain depends on the flour’s protein quantity and quality; higher‑protein flour absorbs more water, so at the same hydration a dough made with higher‑protein flour is tighter

A rule of thumb is that each 1 % increase in protein content shifts water absorption by roughly 2 %; thus 75 % hydration on an 11 % protein flour is comparable to about 78–79 % on a 12.5 % protein flour

High‑hydration dough develops gluten more effectively through rests and stretch‑and‑folds than by intensive kneading, and an autolyse (mixing flour and water before other ingredients) further assists crumb openness
Pushing hydration beyond the dough’s capacity causes the gluten network to fail, resulting in a slack dough that bakes flat and yields a tighter rather than more open crumb
In the author’s trials, increasing hydration from 65 % to 75 % opened the crumb when the bread flour contained sufficient protein
The observed dense, sideways‑spreading crumb with lower‑protein flour matches the described slackening effect of insufficient protein at a given hydration

The resulting loaf measured 11 cm in height, had large holes, a beautifully open crumb with thin cell walls, deep color, and a crisp crust.

The loaf baked from that batch measured 9.5 cm in height and had a fine, even crumb that was described as a little tight, moist but heavy.
High‑hydration dough builds gluten better through rests and folds than through kneading.

An autolyse (flour and water rested first) also helps gluten development in high‑hydration doughs.

## Key points
Bulk fermentation is optimal at 24–27 °C; with 20 % starter the dough typically doubles in 4–5 hours[[source:aee61e21-c410-4a08-9955-96ad3febe9eb]].
Each 1 °C increase speeds fermentation by roughly 10–15%, making fermentation at 28 °C about 30 % faster than at 26 °C[[source:aee61e21-c410-4a08-9955-96ad3febe9eb]].
A 2 °C temperature increase markedly accelerated fermentation, indicating that fermentation time must be shortened at higher temperatures[[source:1bcda75b-e94b-4f65-8885-5017d7aa599c]].
Raising the bulk fermentation temperature from 26 °C to 28 °C while keeping a 4‑hour duration caused over‑fermentation and the dough collapsed[[source:1bcda75b-e94b-4f65-8885-5017d7aa599c]][[source:aee61e21-c410-4a08-9955-96ad3febe9eb]].
At 28 °C the dough volume more than doubled after 3 hours and was over‑blown with large surface bubbles after 4 hours[[source:1bcda75b-e94b-4f65-8885-5017d7aa599c]].
Above 28 °C acid‑producing bacteria dominate, making the dough sour and weakening gluten, so an over‑blown dough collapses easily[[source:aee61e21-c410-4a08-9955-96ad3febe9eb]].
The dough showed little tension during shaping and slumped[[source:1bcda75b-e94b-4f65-8885-5017d7aa599c]].
The baked loaf had a sunken middle, height 8 cm, uneven crumb with large cavities beside dense patches, strong sour flavor, and pale crust[[source:1bcda75b-e94b-4f65-8885-5017d7aa599c]].
When a sourdough starter is allowed to go past its peak (about 4 hours after feeding at ~26 °C), it sinks and becomes sharply sour, a sign of over‑fermentation[[source:9f70dc96-33d7-4590-bb09-af507a92b1a7]].
At a room temperature of 22 °C the starter required 8 hours to double in volume, showing slower fermentation at lower temperatures[[source:9f70dc96-33d7-4590-bb09-af507a92b1a7]].
Using water at 30 °C accelerates starter activity, whereas colder water can delay activity by roughly half a day, demonstrating temperature’s impact on fermentation rate[[source:9f70dc96-33d7-4590-bb09-af507a92b1a7]].
Cold fermentation at 4–6 °C for 8–16 hours nearly stops rise while enzymes continue to develop aroma and sweetness, and the cold dough is easier to shape[[source:aee61e21-c410-4a08-9955-96ad3febe9eb]].
Judge the end of fermentation by dough volume and spring‑back of a poke rather than by preset time, because temperature changes render recipe times unreliable[[source:aee61e21-c410-4a08-9955-96ad3febe9eb]].
A 12‑hour cold fermentation produced better flavor, matching the described benefits of cold fermentation[[source:aee61e21-c410-4a08-9955-96ad3febe9eb]].

The dough was almost liquid at first in trial 1, but after the third fold it tightened and became glossy.
During bulk fermentation the dough doubled in volume within four hours in trial 1.

content.text: The starter amount was 60 g, equal to 20 % of the flour weight.
The starter was added after a 30‑minute autolyse and the dough was kneaded for 10 minutes.

A sourdough starter can be begun with 50 g whole‑wheat flour and 50 g water at about 30 °C, mixed in a loosely covered container and kept at ~26 °C.
Each day after the first, 50 g of the starter is retained and fed with 50 g whole‑wheat flour and 50 g water, with the discard placed in the refrigerator.
By day 3 the starter shows a sour smell and tiny bubbles.
On day 5 the starter doubles in volume about six hours after feeding.
On day 7 the starter doubles in 4–5 hours after feeding and reaches its peak about four hours post‑feeding; after the peak it begins to sink and become sharply sour.
When the ambient temperature drops to 22 °C the doubling time extends to eight hours, showing that starter activity depends strongly on temperature.
Using water at 30 °C accelerates activity, while cold tap water delays it by roughly half a day.

content.text: On day 5 of the starter, the culture doubled in volume six hours after feeding.
By day 7 the starter doubled in four to five hours after feeding and its peak occurred about four hours post‑feeding, after which it began to sink and become sharply sour.
When the ambient temperature fell to 22 °C, the time needed for the starter to double increased to eight hours, indicating that activity depends strongly on temperature.
Using water heated to 30 °C accelerated starter activity, while using cold tap water delayed it by roughly half a day.
By day 3 the starter produced a sour smell and tiny bubbles, showing early signs of fermentation.
Bulk fermentation at 24–27 °C with 20 % starter typically doubles in volume within 4–5 hours, showing faster activity under these temperatures.
Each 1 °C increase in temperature accelerates fermentation by roughly 10–15 %, and at 28 °C the process runs about 30 % faster than at 26 °C.
When the temperature exceeds 28 °C, acid‑producing bacteria dominate, causing the dough to become sour and the gluten to weaken, which can lead to collapse.

content.text: Bulk fermentation is best performed at 24–27 °C; with a 20 % starter the dough typically doubles in volume within 4–5 hours.
Raising the fermentation temperature from 26 °C to 28 °C while keeping a 4‑hour bulk fermentation caused the dough to more than double in volume after 3 hours and become overblown at 4 hours.

At 28 °C the dough showed little tension when shaping, collapsed in the middle during baking, produced an uneven crumb with large cavities and dense patches, and developed a strongly sour, pale crust.
Each 1 °C rise speeds fermentation by roughly 10–15 %; consequently, fermentation at 28 °C runs about 30 % faster than at 26 °C.
A 2 °C increase accelerated fermentation enough that a 4‑hour bulk became too long, implying that higher temperatures require shorter fermentation times.
Above 28 °C the acid‑producing bacteria take over, the dough turns sour, and the acid weakens gluten so an over‑blown dough collapses easily.

At 26 °C bulk fermentation for 4 hours (followed by a 2‑hour proof at the same temperature) produced a loaf 9.5 cm tall with a fine, even crumb that was a little tight, moist but heavy, and the dough was cohesive and easy to handle.
At 26 °C the starter doubled in volume in about 4–5 hours after feeding on day 7 and in about 6 hours after feeding on day 5.
When the ambient temperature dropped to 22 °C the same starter required about 8 hours to double, indicating slower fermentation at lower temperature.
Using water at 30 °C accelerated starter activity, causing faster fermentation compared with cooler water.
Using cold tap water delayed starter development by approximately half a day, reflecting a slowdown due to lower water temperature.
Cold fermentation at 4–6 °C for 8–16 hours nearly stops the rise, but enzymes continue to work, building aroma and sweetness; the cold dough is also easier to shape.
The better flavor of a 12‑hour cold trial matches the cold‑fermentation effect described.
Judge the end of fermentation by the dough’s volume and the spring‑back of a poke rather than by the clock; recipe times become irrelevant once temperature changes.
In a 28 °C, 4‑hour trial the dough collapsed because the clock, not the dough’s state, was used to decide the end; stopping at about 3 hours would have prevented the collapse.

content.text: The bulk fermentation consisted of 2 hours at 26 °C with three folds, followed by 12 hours in the refrigerator at 4 °C
The dough was shaped directly from the refrigerator and then given a final proof of 2 hours at 26 °C
The cold dough was easy to handle and shaped cleanly
During the final proof the dough rose to the rim of the tin within 2 hours
The loaf reached a height of 11 cm, with an open crumb comparable to trial 3 but with more evenly sized holes
